qs.q: A young patient presents with extreme photosensitivity, early-onset skin freckling, and multiple basal cell carcinomas after minimal sun exposure. Which specific DNA repair pathway is most likely defective?
qs.e: Xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by mutations in nucleotide excision repair genes, leading to an inability to fix UV-induced thymine dimers. Transcription-coupled repair is defective in Cockayne syndrome, which presents with premature aging rather than prominent skin cancers.

exam: A 55‑year‑old farmer presents with a 1‑cm pearly nodule on the nose. What is your next step and why? — Perform a punch biopsy to confirm BCC before planning excision, because clinical appearance alone may miss aggressive subtypes.
How does peripheral palisading help differentiate BCC from SCC on histology? — Palisading shows orderly basal cell alignment, whereas SCC shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.

A patient with HIV develops a pigmented facial lesion. Which diagnosis is most likely and what test confirms it? — BCC is common in immunosuppressed patients; a shave biopsy with histology confirms the diagnosis.
Why is Mohs surgery preferred for BCC on the periorbital area? — It provides maximal tissue conservation while ensuring clear margins, preserving function and cosmesis.
What are the indications for radiotherapy in BCC management? — Inoperable lesions, patient refusal of surgery, or recurrent disease where surgery would cause unacceptable morbidity.
A lesion is clinically typical for BCC but biopsy shows only inflammation. What should you do? — Repeat a deeper or excisional biopsy because superficial sampling may miss the tumour.

Explain why topical imiquimod is suitable for superficial BCC but not for morphea‑form BCC. — Imiquimod stimulates local immune response effective for thin lesions; morphea‑form infiltrates deep tissue, requiring surgical removal.

What preventive advice would you give to a community of outdoor workers to reduce BCC risk? — Wear wide‑brim hats, long sleeves, apply broad‑spectrum sunscreen daily, and seek shade during peak UV hours.

ai.summary: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a locally invasive skin cancer arising from basal keratinocytes, driven mainly by UV exposure. It rarely metastasises but can cause significant tissue destruction if untreated.

b: Pearly, translucent nodule with rolled edge
Telangiectasia over lesion
Biopsy: basaloid nests, peripheral palisading
sections.p: A malignant tumour of basal epidermal cells presenting as a pearly papule or nodule with rolled borders and telangiectasia. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by a shave or punch biopsy showing nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading.

b: T1 ≤2 cm, low‑risk site
T2 >2 cm ≤4 cm or high‑risk site
T3 >4 cm or deep invasion, perineural spread
T4 invasion of bone or cartilage
sections.p: BCC is staged using the AJCC 8th edition T‑category based on size, depth, perineural invasion and high‑risk location (e.g., nose, periorbital). Staging guides surgical margins and need for Mohs micrographic surgery.

b: UV‑B induced DNA damage (p53 mutations)
Chronic sun exposure in outdoor workers
Immunosuppression (HIV, organ transplant)
Rare: basal cell nevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome)
sections.p: Chronic ultraviolet (UV) radiation is the dominant cause, especially in fair‑skinned individuals. In low‑resource tropical settings, cumulative sun exposure, outdoor occupations, and lack of protective clothing are common contributors.

b: Pearly nodule with rolled edge
Central ulceration (rodent ulcer)
Pigmented or scar‑like forms
Usually asymptomatic until large
sections.p: Patients notice a slowly enlarging, painless lesion on sun‑exposed skin. Variants include pigmented BCC, ulcerated (rodent ulcer) and morphea‑form (sclerosing) which may appear as a scar‑like plaque.

t.b: Confirms typical morphology; guides biopsy site
Distinguishes BCC from mimics (seborrhoeic keratosis, actinic keratosis)
Assesses deep invasion or perineural spread

b: Rapid growth, pain, or bleeding
Invasion of eye, ear canal, or nasal cartilage
Persistent ulceration with foul discharge
sections.p: Although metastasis is rare, aggressive subtypes can invade bone, cartilage, or orbit, leading to functional loss. Ulceration with secondary infection is a common complication.

b: Excision with 4‑mm margin for low‑risk BCC
Mohs surgery for nose, periorbital, or recurrent lesions
Curettage & electrodessication for small, low‑risk lesions
Topical imiquimod for superficial BCC when surgery unavailable
Radiotherapy for patients unsuitable for surgery
sections.p: First‑line treatment is complete surgical removal with appropriate margins; Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for high‑risk sites. Alternatives include curettage & electrodessication, cryotherapy, topical imiquimod or 5‑fluorouracil, and radiotherapy when surgery is not feasible.

b: Review scar at 3‑month post‑excision
Full skin exam annually thereafter
Educate on UV avoidance and regular self‑examination
sections.p: Patients need skin checks every 6‑12 months for new lesions. Sun‑protective measures (wide‑brim hats, sunscreen, clothing) are essential, especially for outdoor workers.

b: Seborrhoeic keratosis – stuck‑on, waxy appearance
Actinic keratosis – rough, scaly plaque, may progress to SCC
Pigmented BCC vs. malignant melanoma – use dermoscopy and biopsy
Pyogenic granuloma – rapidly growing red papule, bleeds easily
sections.p: Several benign or premalignant lesions mimic BCC clinically.

b: Shallow biopsy → false‑negative for aggressive subtype
Pigmented lesions → mistaken for melanoma without histology
sections.p: Biopsy sampling error can miss the peripheral palisading pattern, leading to under‑diagnosis. Superficial shave may not capture deeper invasive component.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid increase in size, pain, or bleeding
Signs of orbital or cartilage invasion
